theory.what: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is a link-state routing protocol standardized as RFC 2328. Unlike distance-vector protocols (RIP, EIGRP) that share full routing tables with neighbours, OSPF floods Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) to all routers in an area, building a complete topological map called the Link-State Database (LSDB). Every OSPF router then runs Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm independently on that LSDB to compute the shortest path tree to every destination. The result is a loop-free, metric-based routing table where every router converges on the same topology picture. OSPF supports VLSM, CIDR, authentication (MD5/SHA), and classless routing natively. It uses cost as its metric, calculated as the reference bandwidth (100 Mbps by default) divided by the interface bandwidth, giving administrators fine-grained control over path selection.
theory.why: OSPF is the dominant interior gateway protocol (IGP) in enterprise and service provider networks for several reasons. First, its fast convergence: when a link fails, OSPF detects the change within seconds (Hello timer: 10s, Dead timer: 40s) and floods the update network-wide, triggering only affected routers to re-run SPF rather than recalculating everything. Second, its hierarchical design through areas dramatically reduces routing table size and SPF computation for larger networks. Third, OSPF provides loop-free routing intrinsically. Fourth, OSPF is vendor-interoperable. Fifth, LSA types enable advanced capabilities such as route summarization, external route injection, and NSSA partial external injection. Mastering OSPF is required for CCNA, CCNP, JNCIA, and virtually all network engineering certifications and roles.
theory.how: OSPF operation follows a structured five-phase process. Phase 1 — Neighbour Discovery: Routers send Hello packets every 10 seconds (default) to multicast 224.0.0.5 (AllSPFRouters) on broadcast media. Phase 2 — LSA Exchange: Once neighbours reach the 2-Way state, they proceed through ExStart/Exchange states to compare their LSDB summaries. A designated router (DR) and backup designated router (BDR) are elected on broadcast networks to reduce LSA flooding from O(n²) to O(n). Phase 3 — Database Synchronisation: Routers send Link-State Request (LSR) packets and receive Link-State Update (LSU) packets. Phase 4 — SPF Computation: Each router independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm on its LSDB to construct a Shortest Path Tree. Phase 5 — Ongoing Maintenance: Hello packets continue every 10 seconds. OSPF neighbour states: Down → Attempt (NBMA only) → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full.
theory.when: Use OSPF in any network that needs fast convergence, hierarchical scaling, and vendor independence. Typical scenarios include: enterprise campus networks, ISP backbone networks, data centre leaf-spine topologies, multi-vendor environments, and MPLS LDP/TE environments. Use OSPF Area 0 for the backbone transit core, standard areas for leaf connectivity, stub areas to reduce LSA flooding, and NSSA to inject limited external routes. Avoid OSPF in flat networks exceeding 500 routers within a single area, in networks with frequent flapping links, or when sub-second convergence is required (consider IS-IS instead).
key_concepts: Link-State vs Distance-Vector
Dijkstra SPF algorithm
Area hierarchy (Backbone Area 0, standard, stub, NSSA, totally stubby)
LSA Types 1-7 (Router, Network, Summary, ASBR-Summary, AS-External, NSSA)
DR/BDR election on broadcast networks
Hello/Dead timers (10s/40s default)
OSPF cost = 10^8 / interface bandwidth
Router ID selection and manual configuration
ABR (Area Border Router) and ASBR (AS Boundary Router)
Virtual links for connecting discontinuous Area 0
OSPF authentication (MD5, SHA, null)
Passive interfaces
Route summarisation on ABRs
OSPFv3 for IPv6
Graceful restart / NSF for hitless upgrades
theory.configuration:
! OSPF configuration — three-area design
router ospf 1
 router-id 1.1.1.1
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 2
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
 area 1 range 192.168.0.0 255.255.0.0
 area 2 stub no-summary
 timers throttle spf 50 200 10000
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip ospf cost 10
 ip ospf hello-interval 10
 ip ospf dead-interval 40
 ip ospf priority 10
 ip ospf authentication message-digest
 ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 OSPFSecret123
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Setting Up OSPF in a Three-Area Network**
A company has three sites connected via WAN links. The core site uses Area 0, with two remote sites in Area 1 and Area 2.

R1 (Core — Area 0 and ABR):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 1.1.1.1
   network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN to R2
   network 10.0.0.4 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN to R3
   network 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0  ! Core LAN
   area 1 range 192.168.0.0 255.255.0.0   ! Summarize Area 1
   area 2 range 172.17.0.0 255.255.0.0    ! Summarize Area 2

R2 (Remote Site 1 — Area 1):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 2.2.2.2
   network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0       ! WAN link must be Area 0
   network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
   network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 1
   passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1

R3 (Remote Site 2 — Totally Stubby Area 2):
  router ospf 1
   router-id 3.3.3.3
   area 2 stub no-summary
   network 10.0.0.4 0.0.0.3 area 0
   network 172.17.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 2

Verification:
- show ip ospf neighbor → all three routers should show Full state
- show ip route ospf on R2 → should show default route + Area 2 subnets via R1
- show ip route on R1 → should show 192.168.0.0/16 (summarized), not individual /24s

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing OSPF Neighbour Issues**
Symptom: Two routers connected directly won't form OSPF adjacency.

Step 1 — Check L1/L2: ping 10.0.0.2 source 10.0.0.1
Step 2 — Show ip ospf interface Gi0/0: confirm network type, cost, and state
Step 3 — Show ip ospf neighbor:
- Stuck in INIT: mismatched subnet mask or area ID
- Stuck in 2-WAY: waiting for DR/BDR election
- Stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE: MTU mismatch! Fix with 'ip mtu 1500' on both sides and 'clear ip ospf process'

**Worked Example 3: Cost Manipulation**
To prefer a backup link over the primary:
  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   ip ospf cost 100    ! Higher cost = less preferred
Default cost for 100Mbps is 1; setting it to 100 makes the link strongly disfavoured.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• OSPF is a link-state IGP using Dijkstra's SPF algorithm on a complete topology map (LSDB)
• Hello/Dead timers (10s/40s) maintain neighbour relationships; failure triggers fast convergence
• Areas reduce SPF computation — Area 0 is the backbone that all other areas connect to
• OSPF cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth; manipulate cost for traffic engineering
• DR/BDR election reduces flooding on broadcast networks from O(n²) to O(n)
• Set router-id manually, use passive interfaces on access ports, and tune SPF timers for faster convergence
• OSPFv3 runs on IPv6 with per-link (not per-subnet) semantics

**Best Practice:** Configure OSPF on point-to-point links where possible (no DR/BDR election overhead, faster convergence).
troubleshooting: show ip ospf neighbor [detail] — Verify neighbours have reached Full state
show ip ospf database — Inspect LSDB contents per LSA type
show ip ospf interface [name] — Check timers, cost, state, DR/BDR
show ip route ospf — Verify OSPF-learned routes in RIB
show ip protocols — Confirm OSPF process configuration
show ip ospf — Display process ID, RID, SPF stats, areas
debug ip ospf adj — Troubleshoot neighbour adjacency issues in real time
debug ip ospf packet — Analyse incoming/outgoing OSPF packets
clear ip ospf process — Force full OSPF restart (use with caution!)

theory.what: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), defined in RFC 4271, is the path-vector routing protocol that interconnects the autonomous systems (ASes) forming the global internet. Unlike IGPs that care about the lowest-cost path, BGP is a policy-driven protocol where operators select paths based on business relationships and traffic engineering goals expressed through path attributes. BGP operates over TCP (port 179), ensuring reliable incremental updates. Each BGP route carries AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED), and ORIGIN attributes. The global BGP routing table now exceeds 1 million IPv4 prefixes and 200,000 IPv6 prefixes.
theory.why: BGP is the protocol that makes the internet function. Every ISP, cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP), CDN (Cloudflare, Akamai), and large enterprise with multi-homed connectivity runs BGP. BGP enables: (1) multi-homed internet connectivity with traffic engineering using Local Pref and MED; (2) MPLS Layer 3 VPNs and EVPN fabrics; (3) cloud connectivity via Direct Connect and ExpressRoute; (4) fine-grained policy control through path attributes and communities that no IGP can match. Understanding BGP is critical for preventing blackholing and route leaks.
theory.how: BGP operation: Phase 1 — Session Establishment over TCP port 179 with OPEN messages (AS number, Hold Time, capabilities). Phase 2 — Initial UPDATE exchange of all feasible routes. Phase 3 — Incremental updates only after initial exchange. Phase 4 — Best Path Selection (10-step process): Weight → Local Pref → Local Origin → AS Path length → Origin → MED → eBGP/iBGP → IGP metric to next-hop → Age → Router ID. eBGP runs between ASes (TTL=1, AS_PATH loop prevention). iBGP runs within an AS (requires full mesh or route reflectors, split-horizon rules).
theory.when: Deploy BGP for: multi-homed internet connectivity, ISP peering at IXPs, cloud on-ramp (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute), data centre EVPN/VXLAN fabrics (RFC 7938), MPLS VPNs, and large enterprise WANs. Do NOT use BGP for simple internal routing where an IGP suffices — BGP adds complexity, slower convergence (30-90s default), and higher operational overhead.
key_concepts: AS (Autonomous System): unique 16-bit or 32-bit identifier
eBGP (External BGP): between ASes, TTL=1, AS_PATH loop prevention
iBGP (Internal BGP): within AS, requires full mesh or route reflectors
Route Reflector (RR): scales iBGP from O(n²) to O(n)
AS_PATH attribute: sequence of AS numbers for loop detection and path length
Local Preference (LOCAL_PREF): 32-bit integer, higher preferred, controls outbound exit
Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED): 32-bit metric, lower preferred, influences inbound selection
BGP Communities: 32-bit tags for inter-AS signalling (NO_EXPORT, NO_ADVERTISE, LOCAL_AS)
Best Path Selection: 10-step decision process
Prefix filtering with prefix-lists, AS_PATH access-lists, route-maps
BGP convergence: ~90s by default; accelerated via BFD and Fast External Failover
Multiprotocol BGP (MP-BGP): VPNv4, IPv6, EVPN address families
BGP PIC: Prefix Independent Convergence for fast failover
BGP Flowspec: DDoS mitigation via route filtering
Graceful restart / NSF: hitless BGP session restart
theory.configuration:
! eBGP multi-homing configuration
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 10.0.0.1
 bgp log-neighbor-changes
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 description PRIMARY-ISP
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 ebgp-multihop 2
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 update-source Loopback0
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 password BGPSecureKey
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 timers 10 30
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 remote-as 65003
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 description BACKUP-ISP
 neighbor 198.51.100.1 password BGPSecureKey2
 network 10.0.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
 network 192.168.0.0 mask 255.255.0.0
 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF permit 10
  set local-preference 150
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF in
 ip prefix-list ALLOWED permit 10.0.0.0/8 le 24
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED in
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 prefix-list ALLOWED out
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Multi-Homed BGP with Traffic Engineering**
A company has two ISP connections — ISP-A (AS 65002) and ISP-B (AS 65003). They advertise prefix 203.0.113.0/24.

Goal: Prefer ISP-A for outbound and inbound traffic; ISP-B is backup.

Configuration:
- On ISP-A neighbour: apply route-map SET-LOCAL-PREF in (set local-preference 150)
- On ISP-B neighbour: apply route-map PREPEND-AS out (set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001)

Outbound: Traffic leaves via ISP-A (LOCAL_PREF 150 > 100 default)
Inbound: Internet prefers ISP-A because ISP-B's path is longer (65001 65001 65001 65001 vs just 65001)
Failover: If ISP-A fails, BGP withdraws routes and traffic shifts to ISP-B automatically

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing BGP Session Issues**
Symptom: BGP session stuck in Idle state.

Step 1 — ping peer source Loopback0 (TCP reachability)
Step 2 — nc -zv peer 179 (verify TCP port 179 open)
Step 3 — show run | section router bgp (verify remote-as on both sides)
Step 4 — show ip bgp summary (check state: Idle(Pfx)=prefix filter, Active=TCP issue, Idle(NoMem)=memory)
Step 5 — enable 'bgp log-neighbor-changes' for detailed state transitions

**Worked Example 3: BGP Community-Based Route Filtering**
A provider wants to prevent Customer A's routes from reaching Customer B (competitor).

Customer A tags routes: set community 65000:100 + send-community
Provider filters: ip community-list standard NO-CUST-B permit 65000:100
Provider applies: route-map FILTER-IN (match community NO-CUST-B) on Customer B's neighbour inbound.
Routes matching community 65000:100 are not sent to Customer B.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• BGP is a path-vector protocol making policy-based routing decisions using path attributes
• eBGP between ASes; iBGP within AS (full mesh or route reflectors)
• 10-step best path selection: Weight → Local Pref → Local Origin → AS Path → Origin → MED → eBGP/iBGP → IGP Metric → Age → Router ID
• AS_PATH provides loop prevention; LOCAL_PREF controls outbound; MED/AS_PATH prepending influences inbound
• BGP Communities enable scalable inter-AS policy signalling
• Route Reflectors scale iBGP from O(n²) to O(n)
• Default convergence is 30-90s; BFD reduces to milliseconds

**Best Practice:** Use BGP authentication, implement prefix filtering (inbound and outbound), configure BFD for sub-second convergence on critical peering sessions, and use TTL Security (GTSM) for eBGP.
troubleshooting: show ip bgp summary — Quick peer status: Established count, prefixes received, state per peer
show ip bgp [prefix] — Detailed route attributes, path selection tiebreaker steps
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] — Full session details: state, timers, capabilities, prefixes
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] received-routes — What BGP has received (requires soft-reconfiguration inbound)
show ip bgp neighbors [addr] advertised-routes — What BGP is advertising outbound
show ip bgp rib-failure — Routes BGP knows but didn't install in RIB
show ip route bgp — BGP routes in the routing table
show bgp ipv4 unicast summary — IPv4 AF-specific peer summary
debug ip bgp updates — Log BGP UPDATE messages
show ip bgp community — Inspect routes tagged with specific BGP communities
ping peer source Loopback0 — Verify TCP reachability
traceroute peer source Loopback0 — Verify multi-hop path

theory.what: HSRP and VRRP provide gateway redundancy — if the primary router fails, a backup takes over the virtual IP seamlessly. Clients never need to change their default gateway.
theory.why: A single router as default gateway is a single point of failure. FHRP ensures continuous connectivity even when a router fails — essential for high availability.
theory.how: HSRP/VRRP create a virtual IP shared between routers. Active/Master router responds to the virtual IP; Standby/Backup monitors via hello packets; if Active fails, Standby takes over (3-10 seconds). HSRP: Cisco proprietary. VRRP: Open standard (RFC 5798).
theory.when: Use FHRP whenever you have redundant routers/L3 switches serving as default gateways. Required for any HA network design.
key_concepts: Virtual IP (VIP)
Active/Standby (HSRP) or Master/Backup (VRRP)
Priority (higher = preferred)
Preemption
Hello/Hold timers
Interface tracking
theory.configuration:
! HSRP
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.0.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 10.0.10.1
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 20

! VRRP (open standard)
interface Vlan10
 vrrp 1 ip 10.0.10.1
 vrrp 1 priority 110
 vrrp 1 preempt
 vrrp 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 20
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Active/Active HSRP with Load Sharing**
Architecture: Two routers (R1 and R2) both serve as gateways for different VLANs, sharing traffic load while providing failover for each other.

R1:
  interface Vlan10  ! Primary gateway for VLAN 10
   standby 1 ip 10.0.10.1
   standby 1 priority 110  ! Higher priority = Active for VLAN 10
   standby 1 preempt
  interface Vlan20  ! Backup gateway for VLAN 20
   standby 2 ip 10.0.20.1
   standby 2 priority 100  ! Lower priority = Standby for VLAN 20
   standby 2 preempt

R2:
  interface Vlan10  ! Backup gateway for VLAN 10
   standby 1 ip 10.0.10.1
   standby 1 priority 100
   standby 1 preempt
  interface Vlan20  ! Primary gateway for VLAN 20
   standby 2 ip 10.0.20.1
   standby 2 priority 110
   standby 2 preempt

Result: Traffic for VLAN 10 flows through R1, VLAN 20 through R2. If either fails, both VLANs use the remaining router.

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing HSRP Issues**
Symptom: Hosts can't ping the HSRP virtual IP.

Step 1 — Check HSRP state on both routers:
  show standby brief
  Expected output: One router is Active for the group, the other is Standby.
  If both are Active → HSRP split-brain (standby can't reach active — check connectivity between routers).
  If both are Standby → Preempt not configured, or timers are disagreeing.

Step 2 — If state is correct but hosts can't reach VIP:
  Can the Active router reach the virtual IP itself? Try pinging the VIP from the Active router.
  If ping fails, the VIP is not being added to the interface properly. Check standby config.
  Can hosts ping the Active router's real IP? If not, L2 connectivity issue, not HSRP.

Step 3 — Check interface tracking:
  show standby | include tracking
  If the tracked interface (uplink) is down, the priority drops and the other router should become Active.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• HSRP (Cisco) and VRRP (open standard RFC 5798) provide gateway redundancy via a shared virtual IP
• Active/Master router handles traffic; Standby/Backup monitors via hello packets and takes over on failure
• Priority (higher = preferred) and preemption control which router is active
• Interface tracking reduces priority when an uplink fails, triggering failover
• Default failover time is 3-10 seconds; can be reduced with sub-second timers
• Use active/active design by making each router primary for different VLANs

**Best Practice:** Always enable preempt and interface tracking. Use active/active load sharing for better resource utilization. Set timers to sub-second on fast networks for quicker failover.
troubleshooting: show standby — detailed HSRP state, timers, priority, virtual IPs
show standby brief — quick overview of all HSRP groups and their states
show vrrp — VRRP equivalent of show standby
debug standby — real-time HSRP state changes (use carefully)
Check L2 connectivity between routers — HSRP/VVRP uses multicast 224.0.0.2 or 224.0.0.18
Verify interface tracking — if tracked interface is down, priority drops
Check authentication mismatch between routers

theory.what: EtherChannel bundles multiple physical Ethernet links into one logical link (Port-channel interface), providing N × link bandwidth while surviving individual link failures. The connected devices see one logical interface. Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) treats the bundle as a single link, so all member links can forward traffic simultaneously — STP does NOT block the redundant physical links because it only sees the single logical Port-channel. EtherChannel is standardized as IEEE 802.3ad (Link Aggregation Control Protocol — LACP). The technology is called different names by vendors: EtherChannel (Cisco), Link Aggregation (open standard), Bonding (Linux), or Teaming (Windows Server). A single EtherChannel can bundle up to 8 active links (plus up to 8 redundant standby links with LACP), with speeds from 100 Mbps to 400 Gbps per link.
theory.why: EtherChannel solves a fundamental STP limitation: STP blocks redundant links to prevent loops, wasting bandwidth. With 4 × 10 Gbps links between two switches, STP would block 3 of them (30 Gbps wasted). EtherChannel makes STP see these as one link, so all 4 are active — providing 40 Gbps of bandwidth with 4:1 redundancy. Additional benefits: (1) Linear bandwidth scaling — add links without reconfiguring routing protocols or STP; (2) Load balancing — traffic is distributed across member links using a hash algorithm (src/dst MAC, IP, or port); (3) Automatic failover — if a link fails, traffic is redistributed across remaining links in milliseconds; (4) No STP reconvergence — the Port-channel doesn't go down when a member link fails; (5) Cost-effective — use multiple cheap 1 Gbps links instead of upgrading to 10 Gbps hardware.
theory.how: EtherChannel operation has three modes. Mode 1 — LACP (IEEE 802.3ad, open standard, preferred): Uses LACP PDUs to negotiate and manage the bundle. LACP modes: active (initiates negotiation), passive (responds to negotiation but doesn't initiate). At least one side must be active. LACP also supports: system priority (determines which device controls the bundle), port priority (determines which ports are active vs standby), and LACP fast vs slow rate (1s vs 30s hello). Mode 2 — PAgP (Cisco proprietary): Similar to LACP but Cisco-only. Modes: desirable (initiates) and auto (responds). Mode 3 — Static (on mode): No negotiation, just bundle the ports. Not recommended — doesn't detect misconfiguration on the far end. For all modes, member links MUST match: same speed, duplex, VLAN settings, trunk mode (all access or all trunk), native VLAN, and STP settings. The Port-channel assumes the properties of the member interfaces — you configure features (like trunk) on the Port-channel interface, not individual member ports.
theory.when: Deploy EtherChannel in these scenarios: (1) Switch-to-switch links — the most common use, increasing inter-switch bandwidth; (2) Switch-to-server — connect servers with dual NICs for redundancy and bandwidth (requires LACP support in the NIC driver); (3) Switch-to-router — aggregated uplinks from access switches to distribution routers; (4) Data center ToR-to-leaf — 4-8 × 25/100G links between top-of-rack and leaf switches. Do NOT use EtherChannel when: the two sides don't support the same negotiation protocol, or the links have different characteristics (speed, duplex). Maximum 8 active links per EtherChannel on most platforms (some newer platforms support up to 16 or 32).
key_concepts: LACP (802.3ad) — open standard, preferred; uses active/passive modes
PAgP — Cisco proprietary; uses desirable/auto modes
Port-channel — the logical interface representing the bundle
Load balancing — hash-based; options: src-mac, dst-mac, src-dst-mac, src-ip, dst-ip, src-dst-ip
All member links must match — speed, duplex, VLAN, trunk, STP
Max 8 active links per bundle (plus 8 LACP standby)
LACP system priority — determines which device manages the bundle
LACP port priority — determines which ports are active vs standby
On mode (static) — no protocol; risky because misconfigs aren't detected
theory.configuration:
! LACP EtherChannel (Recommended)
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-4
 description Uplink to Core Switch
 channel-group 1 mode active
!
interface Port-channel1
 description LACP to Core-SW
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,99
 spanning-tree guard root

! Configure load balancing method (global)
port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip

! PAgP EtherChannel (Cisco only)
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-2
 channel-group 2 mode desirable
!
interface Port-channel2
 switchport mode trunk

! LACP with standby links
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1-4
 channel-group 1 mode active
 lacp port-priority 100  ! Lower number = higher priority, these are active
!
interface range GigabitEthernet0/5-8
 channel-group 1 mode passive
 lacp port-priority 200  ! Higher = standby

! Verify
show etherchannel summary
show etherchannel port-channel
show lacp neighbor
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Troubleshooting EtherChannel Issues**
Symptom: EtherChannel shows 'err-disabled' or only one link comes up.

Step 1 — Check physical characteristics of all member links:
  show interfaces status | include Gi0/
  All member links MUST have the same speed and duplex. Mixing 100Mbps and 1Gbps won't work.

Step 2 — Check VLAN configuration consistency:
  show interfaces trunk
  All member links must have the same allowed VLAN list. If one link allows VLAN 10-20 and another allows VLAN 10-30, the bundle won't form.

Step 3 — Verify channel-group mode matches between switches:
  If one side is active and the other is passive, LACP works.
  If both sides are passive, LACP never negotiates. Side A must be active or desirable.
  If both sides are active, LACP works.

Step 4 — Check LACP rate:
  By default LACP sends hellos every 30 seconds. Enabling 'lacp rate fast' sends every 1 second. Both sides must match or the bundle may not form.

**Worked Example 2: Load Balancing Behavior**
EtherChannel load balancing uses a hash algorithm over selected fields.

Default hash: src-dst-mac (or src-dst-ip depending on platform)

Scenario: A single TCP file transfer between Server A (MAC: AA:AA:AA:AA:AA:01) and Server B (MAC: BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:01).
  Hash(src-mac XOR dst-mac) % number_of_links = always the same link
  Conclusion: A single flow uses only ONE link. Multiple flows distribute across links.

To verify the hash selection:
  show etherchannel load-balance
  test etherchannel load-balance interface Port-channel1 mac AA:AA:AA:AA:AA:01 BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:01
  Shows which member link a given flow would use.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• EtherChannel bundles up to 8 physical links into one logical link for N × bandwidth + redundancy
• STP sees the bundle as one link, so all member links are active simultaneously
• LACP (802.3ad, open standard) is the preferred negotiation protocol
• All member links must match: speed, duplex, VLAN settings, trunk mode
• Load balancing is per-flow (hash-based), not per-packet — a single flow uses one link
• Automatic failover when a member link goes down (milliseconds, no STP reconvergence)

**Best Practice:** Use LACP active mode for maximum interoperability. Configure features (trunk, allowed VLANs) on the Port-channel interface, not individual member ports. Use lacp rate fast for faster failure detection on critical links.
troubleshooting: show etherchannel summary — quick status: bundled, individual, err-disabled, or suspended
show etherchannel port-channel — Port-channel interface status and member links
show lacp neighbor — LACP peer status, system ID, port priority
show pagp neighbor — PAgP peer status
show etherchannel load-balance — current load balancing algorithm
show interfaces status | include channel — check member link status
Check VLAN consistency — all members must have same trunk configuration
Check speed/duplex consistency — mismatch prevents bundling
err-disabled — usually indicates misconfiguration or physical issue

theory.what: QoS (Quality of Service) is a set of traffic management techniques that prioritizes certain types of data over others during network congestion. Without QoS, all packets are treated equally — during congestion, voice calls drop, video conferences freeze, and critical business transactions stall while bulk downloads continue unaffected. QoS ensures that critical applications receive the bandwidth, latency, jitter, and packet loss guarantees they require. The core mechanisms include: classification (identifying traffic types), marking (tagging packets with priority values), policing/shaping (enforcing bandwidth limits), queuing (holding packets during congestion), and scheduling (deciding which queue to service next). QoS is implemented at Layer 2 (802.1p/CoS) and Layer 3 (DSCP). The Differentiated Services (DiffServ) architecture is the dominant QoS model — it classifies packets at the network edge into a limited number of traffic classes and applies per-hop behaviors (PHB) at each router.
theory.why: QoS is essential because network bandwidth is finite and congestion is inevitable. Without QoS: (1) Voice quality degrades — voice calls drop when competing with file downloads; (2) Video freezes — video conferencing becomes unusable; (3) Critical transactions time out — database updates, financial trades, and API calls fail; (4) Business-critical apps compete with recreational traffic — YouTube competes with SAP; (5) The 'elephant and mice' problem — a few large flows (elephants) can starve many small flows (mice). QoS ensures business outcomes: voice quality (MOS > 4.0), video quality, transaction completion, and fair allocation. For enterprises, QoS is critical on WAN links (the bottleneck). For service providers, QoS enables service differentiation (Gold/Silver/Bronze SLAs). Without QoS, the network is not managing congestion — it is leaving it to chance.
theory.how: QoS implementation follows the 3-step MQC (Modular QoS CLI) process. Step 1 — CLASSIFY: Create class-maps to match traffic. Match based on: ACL, DSCP/CoS values, NBAR (protocol-based), IP precedence, or incoming interface. Example: class-map VOICE matches RTP traffic (UDP ports 16384-32767). Step 2 — POLICY: Create a policy-map that applies actions to each class. Actions include: bandwidth guarantee (bandwidth kbps), priority queue (strict priority for voice), police (limit bandwidth), shape (smooth traffic bursts), set (mark DSCP/CoS), drop (policing). Step 3 — APPLY: Attach the policy-map to an interface with service-policy {input|output}. QoS components in detail include: Classification using ACLs, NBAR (deep packet inspection), or Layer 2/3 markings; Marking by setting DSCP or CoS values at the trust boundary; Queuing using FIFO, WFQ, CBWFQ, or LLQ; Scheduling deciding which queue to serve next; Policing dropping traffic exceeding a configured rate; and Shaping buffering excess traffic to smooth bursts.
theory.when: Implement QoS in these scenarios: (1) WAN links — always! WAN bandwidth is the most expensive and constrained; (2) VoIP deployments — voice calls require less than 150ms latency, less than 30ms jitter, and less than 1% loss; (3) Video conferencing — requires strict QoS guarantees; (4) Multi-service networks — when voice, video, and data share the same links; (5) Data center — QoS for storage traffic (FCoE, iSCSI) and VM migration; (6) Service provider networks — QoS enables SLAs and service differentiation. QoS design principles: (1) Mark at the trust boundary (IP phone, switch access port, or router edge); (2) Queue at WAN edges where congestion occurs; (3) Police at access edges; (4) Use LLQ for real-time traffic; (5) Limit LLQ to 30% of bandwidth; (6) Use CBWFQ for data classes.
key_concepts: DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) — 6-bit field in IP header for packet marking (64 possible values)
Classification — identifying traffic by ACL, NBAR, or existing markings
Marking — setting DSCP/CoS at the trust boundary (near the traffic source)
LLQ (Low Latency Queuing) — strict-priority queue for real-time traffic
CBWFQ (Class-Based Weighted Fair Queue) — guaranteed bandwidth per class
Policing — drop traffic exceeding rate (marked as 'conform'/'exceed'/'violate')
Shaping — buffer excess traffic, smoothing bursts
Trust boundary — where the network trusts packet markings (IP phone to switch port)
NBAR (Network-Based Application Recognition) — DPI for application identification
WRED (Weighted Random Early Detection) — early packet drop to prevent TCP global synchronization

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Voice and Data QoS on a WAN Link**
A 10 Mbps WAN link carries voice, video, and data.

Policy: WAN-EDGE-OUT
- Voice (EF): priority queue, max 1 Mbps (10%)
- Video (AF41): CBWFQ, min 2 Mbps (20%), max 4 Mbps
- Transactional (AF21): CBWFQ, min 3 Mbps (30%)
- Default (DF): fair queue, remaining bandwidth

Results:
- Voice always gets served first (strict priority). If voice exceeds 1 Mbps, excess is dropped.
- Video and transactional data have minimum guarantees. If not used, bandwidth is available to other traffic.
- Default traffic gets a fair share of what is left but cannot starve higher-priority traffic.

**Worked Example 2: Diagnosing QoS Problems**
Symptom: Voice quality is poor despite QoS configuration.

Step 1 — Verify the policy is applied to the correct interface and direction:
  show policy-map interface Serial0/0/0
  Check: service-policy output: WAN-EDGE
  If the policy shows 0 packets classified, voice traffic is not matching the class-map!

Step 2 — Verify classification:
  show class-map VOICE
  Check: match ip dscp ef — does the voice traffic have DSCP EF set?

Step 3 — Check the trust boundary:
  show mls qos interface Gi0/1
  Is the port configured to trust markings from the IP phone?

Step 4 — Check queue drops:
  show policy-map interface Serial0/0/0
  Look for 'queue depth' and 'drops' — if the priority queue is dropping packets, increase LLQ bandwidth percent.

**Worked Example 3: Campus Access Port QoS**
Cisco IP phone connected to switch port with PC daisy-chained through phone:

interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description User-Port-A12 — Phone + PC
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 100
 switchport voice vlan 110
 mls qos trust device cisco-phone
 mls qos trust cos
 auto qos voip cisco-phone

The phone marks voice traffic as CoS 5 (DSCP EF) and data as CoS 0. The switch trusts these markings from the phone device. PC traffic is re-marked to CoS 0. This establishes the trust boundary at the network edge.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• QoS prioritizes critical traffic during congestion using classification, marking, queuing, and scheduling
• LLQ provides strict priority for real-time traffic (voice, video) with bandwidth limits
• CBWFQ guarantees bandwidth for each traffic class with fair sharing of excess
• DSCP (6-bit, 64 values) is the standard packet marking mechanism
• Trust boundary must be established at the edge (IP phone or access switch)
• Police at access edges, shape at WAN edges
• Limit LLQ to 30% of bandwidth to prevent starvation of other traffic

**Best Practice:** Use AutoQoS for initial setup on Cisco devices, then tune based on monitoring. Always verify QoS with 'show policy-map interface' to confirm packets are matching expected classes.
troubleshooting: show policy-map interface — verify applicable policies, classified packet count, drops per queue
show class-map — review classification criteria
show mls qos interface — check trust state and QoS settings on switch ports
show queueing interface — view queue depths and drop statistics
Verify DSCP values end-to-end using packet capture
Check priority queue drops — indicates LLQ is undersized for voice/video traffic
Verify bandwidth allocation does not exceed interface bandwidth
Check shaping — excessive drops indicate shaper is too restrictive
